messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 25-year-old surgical resident who came for treatment after months of telling herself that what happened overseas should have stayed there. During her military deployment, she had been part of a forward surgical team working close to active combat. The moment that returns most forcefully came during a mass-casualty response when rotor wash hammered the canvas above the aid station and the thudding chop of a helicopter seemed to sit inside her chest. She remembers dropping to the ground beside a wounded service member, her gloves and uniform pressed into a rough, gritty surface she can still feel on her palms and knees, and then a blast so loud it seemed to split the scene open. What stands out is not a tidy sequence but a sensory assault: the aircraft overhead, the bang, the feel of that texture under her hands, and a certainty that she was about to die. Even now, when she tries to describe it in session, she stops and shakes her head. She says she cannot get it into words properly; the memory arrives as terror and sensation before language.

In the months after returning to the United States, she noticed that the memory did not stay in the past. A helicopter passing over the hospital helipad, a sudden bang from equipment being dropped in an operating room, even brushing against a particular rough fabric or surface could bring the whole scene back without warning. It was not like ordinary remembering. For Amina, those moments felt as if she were back in the field hospital with the same panic and bodily alarm she had felt then, as though the event were happening again rather than being recalled. Because the memory itself remained largely sensory and hard to narrate, these sounds and textures seemed to reach straight into it; she often felt ambushed by the full force of the experience before she had even registered what had set it off.

Working as a surgeon has made these reactions impossible to keep at the edges of her life. Entering the hospital each day, she now automatically identifies exits, notes where she could move if something happened, and chooses seats in conference rooms with her back to the wall so she can see everyone coming and going. In the operating room lounge, if a helicopter can be heard approaching the helipad, she feels her body tighten and her eyes begin sweeping the space for danger before she is even fully aware of doing it. Sudden bangs from metal trays or equipment make her flinch and orient immediately toward the source. She tells herself these habits are necessary, the only way to stay ahead of whatever might happen, and they have become especially fixed in places where she cannot control the noise around her.

Over time, though, the constant preparation has made the world feel more perilous rather than less. Because she is always scanning rooms, checking corners, and mentally rehearsing how she would get out, she notices every aircraft sound and every sharp noise. On days when she is especially focused on where the exits are and who is behind her, the chop of helicopter blades from the roof seems louder, more distinct, impossible to ignore. Her attention catches on the very cues she dreads. Sitting rigidly with her back against the wall in the cafeteria, she tracks movements and sounds until a dropped pan or the scrape of a rough chair leg can jolt her into the edge of the old memory. The strategies she relies on to feel safe end up keeping those triggers in the foreground of her day.

This has gradually narrowed her life at work and outside it. She arrives early to unfamiliar rooms so she can choose where to sit. She avoids relaxing in staff spaces unless she can position herself to watch the door. Colleagues have noticed that she startles at bangs and that her eyes move constantly around the room during meetings, and she has become more socially withdrawn rather than explain herself. She is single and lives alone, and at home she still catches herself mapping exits in restaurants or public places before she can settle. What frightens her most is not only the memory itself but the sense that it can be summoned instantly by a sound, a texture, a split second she cannot predict.

She sought help after freezing briefly in the hospital when a helicopter descended as a metal instrument bin clattered nearby, leaving her shaken and ashamed before a case. She is afraid that if this continues, she will lose her confidence in the one place she has always felt most competent. More than anything, Amina wants to be able to hear a helicopter, feel ordinary surfaces, and remain in the present instead of being thrown back into terror she still cannot fully put into words.
